<explanation>
Based on the file structure and README content, this project is a full‐stack application that generates customizable metrics images for GitHub profiles, repositories, organizations, and even individual users. It is built around a highly modular, plugin‐ and template‐driven architecture. Here are the main points and guidelines for creating an accurate system design diagram of this project:

1. Identify the main components of the system:
   • Core Application: This is implemented in the “source/app” directory and is divided into sub-components:
     - Action Runner (“source/app/action”): Handles execution as a GitHub Action, triggered by workflows.
     - Metrics Processor (“source/app/metrics”): This module aggregates data by invoking plugins, processing GitHub API responses (both GraphQL and REST), and applying business logic.
     - Web Server (“source/app/web”): Serves the rendered metrics images and static assets (JS, CSS, HTML) for embedding and viewing.
   • Plugins Module: Located in “source/plugins”, it includes many individual plugins (for achievements, activity, languages, stargazers, etc.). Each plugin contains logic (often in ES modules) plus GraphQL query files that encapsulate specific functionality. This forms the extensibility point of the architecture.
   • Templates Engine: Found in “source/templates” with several sub-folders such as “classic”, “repository”, “terminal”, and “markdown”. These templates (using EJS and CSS) define the visual layout of the generated metrics.
   • CI/CD and Deployment: 
     - GitHub Actions and workflows (under .github/workflows and .github/actions) where automated builds, tests, releases, and even cleaning scripts are defined.
     - Docker integration (via Dockerfile and Docker-related scripts) and deployment configuration (vercel.json) indicating multiple deployment strategies including self-hosting and shared instances.
   • Configuration & Metadata:
     - Several configuration files (e.g., package.json, settings.example.json, .editorconfig, ARCHITECTURE.md) support the overall setup, linting, build, and deployment processes.

2. Define relationships and interactions:
   • When running, the GitHub Action (or a direct command via CLI/Docker) triggers the Metrics Processor. This module calls various plugin modules to retrieve GitHub analytics data by using GitHub APIs (both REST and GraphQL).
   • The aggregated data is then fed into the templating engine. Depending on the template chosen (classic, repository, terminal, markdown, or community), the templating engine renders the final metrics as SVG or HTML.
   • The Web Server sub-component serves these rendered assets as static files that can be embedded or viewed directly by users.
   • CI/CD components (GitHub Actions workflows, scripts under .github/scripts, and Docker setups) automatically test, build, and deploy the code and templates.
   • The plugin system allows easy extensibility: new plugins can be added into the “source/plugins” directory, and each follows a similar structure (e.g., index.mjs, metadata.yml, queries directory) indicating a standardized plugin contract.

3. Highlight important architectural patterns and technologies:
   • Modular Plugin Architecture: The plugins are loosely coupled, and the core system dynamically loads these modules at runtime.
   • Template/Renderer Pattern: The separation between content (the raw metrics data) and appearance (templates) enables customization and theming.
   • CI/CD Integration: The repository is well-integrated with GitHub Actions for continuous testing, code quality, and deployment.
   • Technology Stack: The project is based on Node.js (using ES modules, .mjs files), uses Docker for containerization, and leverages GitHub’s API (both REST and GraphQL) extensively.

4. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram:
   • For this full-stack application, make sure to illustrate the separation between backend processing (GitHub Action and Metrics Processor), plugin integration, and frontend/template rendering.
   • Indicate the external dependency interactions with GitHub’s API, third-party services (like PageSpeed, Leetcode, etc. via social plugins), and even integration with CI/CD pipelines.
   • Use distinct colors or shapes to differentiate:
     - Core modules (action, metrics, web app) versus optional/extension parts (plugins, templates)
     - Deployment/CI components (GitHub Actions workflows, Docker container) versus runtime components.

5. Recommended diagram elements:
   • Components:
       - Label a “GitHub Action / CLI Runner” block that triggers the process.
       - A “Metrics Processor” block that aggregates data.
       - A “Plugin Manager” block (or multiple blocks) showing various plugins (each labeled by their function like “Achievements”, “Languages”, “Stargazers”, etc.).
       - A “Template Engine” block that shows choices of templates (Classic, Repository, Terminal, Markdown, etc.).
       - A “Web Server / Renderer” block that outputs the final SVG/HTML.
       - An “External APIs” block representing GitHub APIs (REST/GraphQL) and other third-party services.
       - CI/CD block showing GitHub Actions and Docker deployment pipelines.
   • Arrows:
       - Use directional arrows to depict data flow from the Action Runner to the Metrics Processor which then interacts with plugins, feeds data to the Template Engine, and outputs the final rendered asset through the Web Server.
       - Show bi-directional arrows between the Metrics Processor and external GitHub APIs.
   • Labels and color coding:
       - Clearly label each component and transition.
       - Use distinct color coding or shapes to distinguish between “runtime” (processing, rendering) components and “development” (CI/CD, testing, deployment) components.

By following these guidelines, you can draw a detailed system design diagram that accurately represents the architecture of this metrics-generation project. Remember that clarity in labeling, clear representation of directional data flows, and a separation of concerns (core app, plugins, templates, and external integrations) are key to capturing the project’s essence. This detailed diagram will serve as a good reference for both current and future developers working on the project.
</explanation>
